questions.question: Which of the following best explains why NAT alone could not fully solve the IPv4 address exhaustion problem?
options: NAT consumes excessive bandwidth due to header expansion
NAT increases end-to-end delay in wireless networks
NAT requires a dedicated subnet for every device
NAT breaks transparency and hampers protocol innovation
NAT mandates IPv6-style 128-bit addresses internally

questions.question: Which of the following IPv6 features directly improves support for end-to-end connectivity compared to IPv4?
options: Variable-length addressing
Multiple simultaneous link-local addresses
Per-hop source routing
Default tunneling via IPv4 NAT
Stateless address autoconfiguration

questions.question: What is a key design benefit of IPv6 address formatting for modern applications?
options: It embeds transport-layer headers into IP addresses
It simplifies parsing by embedding TCP flags
It avoids the use of hexadecimal representation
It allows for hierarchical address delegation
It eliminates the need for DNS

questions.question: Which of the following would result in an invalid IPv6 compressed address representation?
options: Using "::" more than once in a single address
Including leading zeros in a segment
Using "::" to compress a single contiguous block of zeros
Mixing decimal and hexadecimal notation in the same address
Omitting a non-zero segment using "::"

questions.question: Which of the following best distinguishes anycast from multicast in IPv6?
options: Anycast delivers packets to all nodes, multicast delivers to one
Anycast uses TCP only, multicast uses UDP
Anycast and multicast share the same address prefix
Anycast uses routing to the nearest member, multicast to all group members
Anycast requires tunnel encapsulation, multicast does not

questions.question: Which mechanism allows an IPv6 host to configure its address without contacting a DHCP server?
options: DNS-based prefix negotiation
Stateless address autoconfiguration based on MAC
Reverse DNS probing
Router advertisement tunneling
Hop-by-hop header compression

questions.question: What risk is introduced when IPv6 endpoints communicate through an IPv4-only network?
options: Unpredictable MTU negotiation
Failure of end-to-end IPv6 connectivity
Inconsistent use of DNSSEC signatures
IPv6 address collisions
Loss of transport-layer header integrity

questions.question: Which of the following best explains how IP tunneling facilitates IPv6 deployment?
options: It enables Ethernet frames to be carried over IP
It compresses headers to reduce packet size across links
It eliminates the need for DNS during address resolution
It transforms TCP into a connectionless protocol
It allows IPv6 packets to traverse non-IPv6-capable networks

questions.question: What is the primary design motivation for using extension headers in IPv6?
options: To include routing information in Ethernet headers
To allow IP fragmentation at intermediate routers
To remove the need for a transport-layer checksum
To enable compression of repetitive header fields
To simplify the fixed base header and modularize options

questions.question: Why does IPv6 mandate support for a 1280-byte MTU, even if the link MTU is smaller?
options: To avoid the need for congestion control
To simplify DNS query responses
To guarantee minimal packet size across the path
To reduce reliance on router-based address translation
To ensure compatibility with legacy IPv4 routers

questions.question: Why is IPv6 fragmentation only allowed at the source rather than at intermediate routers?
options: IPv6 prohibits fragmentation of any packets
Fragmentation is too computationally expensive for routers
Routers lack access to destination MAC addresses
IPv6 relies on TCP to handle all retransmissions
Source fragmentation reduces router complexity and enhances performance

questions.question: In a multi-hop wireless IPv6 path with 10% packet drop per hop, which risk arises from relying on fragmentation?
options: Each router must reassemble packets before forwarding
Fragmentation triggers ICMP redirects on every hop
TCP resets all connections after loss
Only one fragment needs to be lost to make the full packet unrecoverable
Multiple copies of each fragment flood the network

questions.question: Why might link-layer acknowledgments be insufficient for ensuring delivery in IPv6?
options: Acks are incompatible with multicast traffic
Link-layer acks only work on Ethernet, not wireless
End-to-end delivery depends on higher-layer recovery, not just hop-by-hop acks
IPv6 does not support retransmissions at all
IPv6 disables hop-by-hop header processing

questions.question: What weakened the urgency for IPv6 deployment despite the threat of IPv4 address exhaustion?
options: NAT and address reuse enabled continued IPv4 scalability
ISPs were required to disable IPv4 routing
The IETF deprecated DNS root zone support for IPv4
IPv6 lacked support for high-speed hardware forwarding
IPv6 caused incompatibility with Ethernet devices

questions.question: What is the primary challenge addressed by the 6LoWPAN adaptation of IPv6?
options: Assigning static IPs to devices in industrial plants
Routing over non-IP-capable physical media
Compressing IPv6 headers for small-MTU low-power links
Managing TCP congestion in high-speed datacenters
Preventing DNS leakage in sensor networks

questions.question: Which 6LoWPAN header compression mode reduces an IPv6 address to zero bits?
options: Dynamic prefix shifting
Stateless SAM/DAM = 00 mode
Stateless compression using 64-bit identifiers
Stateful CID-based address negotiation
Link-local address inference from MAC

questions.question: How does IPv6 multicast improve efficiency compared to unicast replication?
options: It reduces redundant packet transmissions over shared links
It uses IPv4 tunnels for backward compatibility
It guarantees reliable delivery to all recipients
It requires receiver-side NAT translation
It assigns separate MTUs per multicast group

questions.question: Which factor contributes most to the limited deployment of inter-domain IP multicast?
options: Complexity of maintaining multicast state in routers
IPv6's incompatibility with Ethernet frames
Cost of leasing multicast-capable IP prefixes
Requirement for symmetric TCP handshakes
Lack of DNSSEC validation for multicast groups

questions.question: What is the defining operational characteristic of anycast communication in IPv6?
options: All receivers in the group send coordinated responses
Each packet is explicitly broadcast to the entire group
The destination is dynamically changed at application layer
Routing delivers packets to one topologically closest node
Packets are fragmented across all destinations

questions.question: What is a primary drawback of supporting anycast at the IP layer?
options: Incompatibility with encrypted HTTPS sessions
Anycast addresses require full packet reassembly at each hop
Routing tables must maintain multiple /32 entries for a single service
Excessive use of DNS queries to resolve routes
Explosion of /8 prefixes in BGP route tables

questions.question: How does anycast help reduce the impact of distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks?
options: By blocking traffic at layer 2 switches
By throttling packets based on TTL expiration
By encrypting all incoming traffic
By spreading malicious traffic across multiple geographically dispersed nodes
By tunneling packets through private VPNs

questions.question: What advantage does IP-layer anycast offer for services deployed across continents?
options: Reduces need for autonomous system (AS) numbers
Ensures deterministic routing paths for all packets
Eliminates the use of DNS for service discovery
Enables user requests to be served by the closest regional server
Guarantees delivery using TCP congestion control

questions.question: Which of the following best summarizes the role of IPv6 in modern networking?
options: It replaces transport protocols like TCP and UDP
It fragments traffic at every intermediate router to improve performance
It eliminates the need for DNS or DHCP in most networks
It uses MAC-layer identifiers to generate encryption keys
It provides a scalable addressing and packet structure with improved support for mobility, security, and QoS

questions.question: Which factor has most significantly delayed global IPv6 adoption?
options: Hardware limitations in core routers
Lack of global DNS support for IPv6
Absence of a 64-bit addressing standard
Compatibility barriers with IPv4 and reliance on NAT
High latency of IPv6 packet forwarding

questions.question: Which transition approach allows IPv6 nodes to communicate across IPv4-only intermediate networks?
options: Multipath routing with DNS failover
Hop-by-hop source-based rerouting
IP-in-IP tunneling over IPv4
IPv6 header compression via CIDR
Dual-stack NAT traversal

questions.question: What is the intended purpose of the IPv6 Flow Label field?
options: To distinguish multicast from unicast traffic
To prioritize DNS resolution requests in the router queue
To identify the next-hop router along a path
To carry session state between transport endpoints
To classify packets belonging to the same flow for consistent forwarding

questions.question: How does the IPv6 'Next Header' field support extensibility?
options: It reserves bits in every header for proprietary encryption
It replaces checksum fields in upper layers
It bypasses the need for address resolution protocols
It allows nested transport-layer protocols without fragmentation
It enables a flexible chain of headers specifying routing and options

questions.question: Why might a "jumbogram" be used in IPv6 networking?
options: To allow for secure broadcast authentication
To support payloads exceeding 65,535 bytes
To transport legacy 802.3 Ethernet frames over IPv6
To carry DNSSEC zone transfers in a compressed format
To perform rapid handover during mobility events

questions.question: In a typical unicast IPv6 address, what does the high-order prefix (e.g., /48 or /64) identify?
options: The network to which the host is attached
The flow label for transport-layer mapping
The packet's hop limit
The transport protocol in use
The checksum of the interface identifier

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is necessary for stateless IPv6 address autoconfiguration to work?
options: The client must manually set its interface ID
The router must send periodic router advertisements
The DNS server must be anycast-enabled
The host must run a local DHCP server
The link must support TCP header compression
